﻿Status (Track C packet): STARTED, not complete yet. I pulled the full brief from BRG-1773525439272 and reviewed Plato’s Phase-2 field/copy audit + pure extraction (34 defects + full field inventory). I then began the external research layer: gathered comparable wording/help-text patterns and authoritative references for confusing terms (TDH / pipe-run distance measurement, heater sizing inputs like wind exposure & covers, electrical panel load framing).

Key sources captured so far:
- NN/g calculator UX guideline emphasizing “offer to explain the purpose of inputs” (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/recommendations-calculator/)
- PNNL/Building America electrical panel calculator copy tying square footage + panel amps to NEC-based load estimation and warning it’s an estimate (https://basc.pnnl.gov/hpwh_installation_tool/electrical_calculator)
- Pentair heat-pump calculator disclaimers listing environmental variables (wind, sun exposure, humidity, plumbing length, etc.) (https://www.pentair.com/en-us/pool-spa/education-support/homeowner-support/calculators/heat-pump-calculator.html)
- Pool Warehouse heater calculator framing (asks current vs desired temp + gives heat-up-time expectation) (https://www.poolwarehouse.com/pool-heater-calculator/)
- Located municipal “Simplified TDH Worksheet” PDFs (e.g., volusia.org / stpetebeach.org) for permitting-context phrasing that can justify measurement guidance language.

What I worked on today: I shifted from “inside” terminology to “outside” language. Instead of inventing definitions, I collected real-world patterns for how other calculators and permitting resources explain the same inputs (why we ask, how to measure, what happens if you guess). That’s the missing complement to Plato’s internal defect list.

What it meant: This is about trust. The OmniPools calculator is powerful, but field ambiguity causes silent garbage-in/garbage-out. The research layer’s job is to anchor each confusing field in language that matches how designers/homeowners actually think on site (two points, a tape measure, and imperfect info) and to back it with recognizable external wording so the UI feels credible.

What drove me: urgency + accountability. The deadline is real, and Plato already produced a high-quality internal audit; my work has to make his fixes easy to implement and defensible (“this is how permitting worksheets / major manufacturers phrase it”). Next step is to write the actual 10–20-item packet in the required format, using Plato’s highest-severity clusters as the spine, and attach citations + “clarify first” top-5 list.
